case_analysis.thread_summary: This thread covers a Sharp [COMPANY]-style customer's Bluetooth SIG certification project for a new device using a surface-mount Bluetooth module, spanning planning through pre-test coordination from December 2024 to March 2025. Early messages discuss whether the customer can reuse another company's certified Host Subsystem QD-ID (advised against) and the resulting decision to combine a certified Controller Subsystem QDID with a purchased certified Host Subsystem stack. Mid-thread discussion evaluates a stack vendor's 3-month porting quote against the option of reusing an already-certified BlueZ-based stack. The latter portion of the thread works through pre-test clarifications for an RF 2-item test: distinguishing it from the RF PHY test, defining 'Testing Voltage' for a USB-PD-powered product, and defining 'cable loss' for an integrated antenna assembly. The thread ends with scheduling for the RF 2-item test.
case_analysis.key_technical_discussion: The discussion covers six linked qualification topics: (1) the risk of referencing an unrelated company's certified Host Subsystem QD-ID without permission; (2) the need for an RF 2-item test (TX power, RX sensitivity) to validate a PCB-routed antenna pattern even when Controller and Host subsystems are independently certified; (3) comparing the lead time of porting a generic host stack versus reusing an already-certified BlueZ-based stack (QDID:149875); (4) distinguishing 'RF test' 2-items from the separate 'RF PHY test' 2-items, including equipment (UART-RS232 cable) and questionnaire scope; (5) defining 'Testing Voltage' for a USB-PD product that negotiates from 5V to 9V; and (6) defining 'cable loss' as the added test/conversion cable's loss (not the antenna's integrated cable), with a 0.6dB default.
case_analysis.key_decision_logic: Throughout, the consultant distinguishes between what is formally possible on paper and what creates downstream qualification risk - e.g., QD-ID reuse may be submittable but risks later cancellation by the actual owner. RF testing requirements are scoped to the actual hardware change (an antenna pattern added on the product PCB) and to the correct test category ('RF test' vs 'RF PHY test') rather than to surface-level terminology matches. Test parameters such as Testing Voltage and cable loss are consistently defined in terms of what is physically supplied to or connected to the DUT during the test, requiring translation from the customer's product-level specs (AC rating, integrated antenna+cable datasheet) into test-level values, with documented defaults (e.g., 0.6dB cable loss) used when a precise spec is unavailable.
case_analysis.risk_if_done_wrong: If the customer had registered using an unauthorized reference to another company's QD-ID, the SIG could cancel the registration at the Listing Owner's request once noticed. If the RF 2-item test were skipped on the assumption that certified Controller and Host subsystems were sufficient, the antenna pattern added on the product's own PCB would go unverified. Misclassifying the RF test as an RF PHY test (or vice versa) could lead to unnecessary equipment preparation (e.g., UART-RS232 cable) or missing questionnaire sections. Misreporting Testing Voltage (e.g., using the AC rating instead of the actual USB-PD-negotiated DC supply) or cable loss (using the antenna's integrated cable loss instead of the test/conversion cable's loss) could produce a test setup or report that doesn't reflect the product's real operating condition.
case_analysis.consulting_takeaway: When a customer proposes combining certified components or referencing existing QDIDs, check both (a) whether referencing an external QD-ID is actually permitted/owned, and (b) whether any hardware change on the customer's own board - such as an antenna pattern routed through the PCB - still requires a targeted RF test, even if the certified building blocks themselves are exempt from re-testing. When explaining RF test parameters (Testing Voltage, cable loss, RF test vs RF PHY test scope), always frame them in terms of what is physically measured or connected to the DUT during the test, since customers naturally map these terms onto product-level specs (AC rating, integrated antenna+cable datasheets) that don't directly translate.
